clinician.trajectory_summary: A 26-year-old female of Hispanic descent presented with recurrent, severe chest pain (7/10 intensity) that had been occurring intermittently since age 17, characterized as sharp and stabbing, associated with heartburn, and responsive to antacids. Two episodes occurred within two weeks prior to admission, representing an increase in frequency that prompted hospitalization. On admission, laboratory evaluation revealed significant inflammation: elevated white blood cell count (12.8 × 10⁹/L), elevated C-reactive protein (1.3 mg/dL), and markedly elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (79 mm/hour). CT angiography of the abdomen and pelvis with contrast demonstrated extensive wall thickening along the descending thoracic aorta and suprarenal abdominal aorta with mild narrowing of the aortic lumen. PET-CT imaging revealed significant metabolic activity in the descending aorta extending to the subclavian arteries, iliofemoral arteries, and popliteal arteries, indicating active vasculitis affecting multiple large vessels. These imaging findings combined with elevated inflammatory markers were diagnostic of Takayasu arteritis, a large-vessel vasculitis. Rheumatology initiated immunosuppressive therapy with prednisone at 1 mg/kg (80 mg daily), methotrexate 20 mg weekly, Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia prophylaxis with trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole, and folic acid supplementation.

ruled_out_or_less_likely_alternatives.basis: While initial symptoms were associated with heartburn and responsive to antacids, the marked elevation in inflammatory markers (ESR 79 mm/hour, CRP 1.3 mg/dL), imaging evidence of extensive aortic wall thickening and narrowing, and PET-CT evidence of active vasculitis in multiple large vessels are inconsistent with primary GERD or peptic ulcer disease. The systemic inflammatory process and large-vessel involvement indicate a vasculitic etiology rather than primary gastrointestinal pathology.

ruled_out_or_less_likely_alternatives.alternative: Coronary artery disease or acute coronary syndrome
ruled_out_or_less_likely_alternatives.basis: The imaging findings of extensive aortic wall thickening, narrowing, and metabolic activity in the descending aorta, subclavian, iliofemoral, and popliteal arteries indicate a systemic large-vessel vasculitis rather than localized coronary disease. The pattern of involvement affecting the aorta and multiple branch vessels is characteristic of Takayasu arteritis, not atherosclerotic coronary disease.
